catalog_quote: Cross-linguistically, the edge of a word is a prominent position (Yip, 2002, 83). This is especially so in Southeast Asia, where iambicity is common (Michaud, 2012). In this context, structurally reduced presyllables are common, as are the diachronic processes that give rise to them (Gehrmann, 2022b, 6). Presyllables are common in Hmong-Mien, and Saxe (2021, 6) describes them for Pa Then. My auditory impression is that the right edge (final) of the word is prominent in Pa Then. Therefore, it is expected that the NFSs are not as likely as final syllables to bear the full realization of a tone. To investigate this, NFSs in different environments are compared, and NFSs are compared to finals. new_statements.rule_in_words: Pa Then (Vietnamese Pa-Hng) is a 7-8-tone language; within (di/sesqui-syllabic) words prominence is on the final syllable (right edge, iambic pattern), while non-final syllables - especially the frequent prefix/presyllables ʔa, ta, ka, tə - are prosodically non-prominent and show reduced tonal realization (acoustically confirmed for ka). The prominence claim itself is the author's auditory impression, supported indirectly by the instrumental finding that tones are realized most fully in monosyllables and final syllables and least fully in presyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; author notes ʔa, ta, tə could not be shown acoustically to differ from ordinary non-final A-tone syllables (only ka demonstrably reduced); data from a single adult male speaker of one Vietnamese locality.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (disyllabic compounds and prefix+root words from a recorded wordlist, i.e. citation forms); statement concerns prominence/tonal realization by position, not a phonemic stress contrast. Second-hand support: Mortensen 2003 (review of Mao & Li 1997) calls the Pahng noun prefixes 'iambic'; Ratliff 2010:199 says Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes are unstressed (family-general).
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 2024 describes Pa Then (Pà Thẻn) of Vietnam from a recorded wordlist of one adult male speaker at an unnamed 'third' Vietnamese locality (distinct from Tân Trịnh and Bắc Quang/Hồng Quang described by Niederer 1997 and Edmondson & Gregerson 2001); all are Vietnamese Pa-Hng = pahn1237 (no separate dialect glottocode). The Chinese varieties (Wenjie 文界, Gundong 滚董, Baiyun 白云) are covered only by Mao & Li 1997 / Chen 1996 (not accessible) and Niederer 1997 (silent on stress). Note Williamson's own Glottolog citation mistakenly points to wuna1248 (Hm Nai/Wunai), but the language studied is Pa Then.
